prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. said Sunday that it is buying troubled Wall Street firm Bear Stearns, amid deepening fears that Bear's demise could have sent shockwaves across already shaky financial markets. The deal to buy Bear Stearns is worth an estimated $236 million. The deal values Bear Stearns at $236 million, or just $2 a share. Shares had closed at $30 on Friday, down 47 percent that day. "Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations," said a statement released Sunday by JPMorgan. Shareholders must approve the deal, which is expected to close by the end of June. JPMorgan is taking immediate responsibility for Bear's trading obligations and assuming "management oversight" of the firm's operations. The deal has already been approved by the Federal Reserve and other regulators, according to the statement. The Fed is providing special emergency financing for up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets. "JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns," said Jamie Dimon, chairman and chief executive of JPMorgan. "Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing ... risk," he continued. The fast-track deal is expected to close by the end of June, the statement said. Bear Stearns was on the brink of financial collapse Friday when JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said they would provide the brokerage a short-term loan. Bear was dealing with a classic "run on the bank." The firm's short-term creditors refused to lend the firm any more money and simultaneously demanded repayment of outstanding debt. The one-two punch overwhelmed Bear's cash position. With the global credit crisis worsening, the Fed -- along with officials from the Treasury Department and other government agencies -- took the dramatic action to prevent the investment bank from going under and igniting widespread panic through the financial markets.  Watch a discussion on the impact on global markets » . Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson said on Sunday that talks about how to rescue Bear had continued throughout the weekend. He defended the Fed's bailout on Friday as "the right decision" and said the Bush administration was ready to take other actions to bring stability to the financial markets. He would not say what might have happened had the government failed to step in. "I'm not going to speculate about what-ifs," he said. "I'm just going to say our clear priority right now -- our number one priority, everything we're doing in the economic arena -- is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy." Bear Stearns has approximately 14,000 employees worldwide. The deal marks an inglorious chapter for 85-year-old Bear Stearns, a storied Wall Street firm the unraveling of which has been fast and furious. Rumors that Bear Stearns was on the verge of collapse started buzzing around Wall Street trading desks last Monday. Chief Executive Alan Schwartz -- who took over as CEO in early January from longtime chief Jimmy Cayne -- appeared on television on Wednesday afternoon to reassure the markets that the firm was stable. But by Thursday night, Bear was in a severe crunch. Some firms that trade with it effectively stopped offering it credit because they feared that Bear was running short of short-term funding, or liquidity. "The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns," said Alan Schwartz, president and CEO of Bear Stearns. "This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances." White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson has briefed U.S. President George W. Bush on the Federal Reserve's role in helping to facilitate the purchase. "We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening," said Fratto. "Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments." Shares of Bear Stearns opened last week at $69.75 and traded as high as $159 last year. E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L1:
**NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) —** JPMorgan Chase & Co. announced Sunday that it would acquire troubled Wall Street firm Bear Stearns, amid mounting fears that Bear’s collapse could send shockwaves through already fragile financial markets.

The transaction is valued at an estimated $236 million, or just $2 per share. Bear Stearns shares had closed at $30 on Friday after falling 47 percent that day.

“Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations,” JPMorgan said in a statement released Sunday.

The transaction, which remains subject to shareholder approval, is expected to close by the end of June. In the meantime, JPMorgan is assuming immediate responsibility for Bear Stearns’ trading obligations and providing “management oversight” of the firm’s operations.

According to the statement, the deal has already received approval from the Federal Reserve and other regulators. The Fed is also providing special emergency financing for up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets.

“JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns,” said Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan’s chairman and chief executive. “Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing ... risk,” he continued.

The fast-tracked transaction is expected to close by the end of June, the statement said.

Bear Stearns was on the brink of financial collapse Friday when JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York announced that they would provide the brokerage with a short-term loan.

Bear was facing a classic “run on the bank”: the firm’s short-term creditors refused to lend it additional money while simultaneously demanding repayment of outstanding debt. This one-two punch overwhelmed Bear’s cash position.

As the global credit crisis worsened, the Fed—along with officials from the Treasury Department and other government agencies—took the dramatic step of intervening to prevent the investment bank from failing and triggering widespread panic across financial markets.

*Watch a discussion on the impact on global markets »*

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson said Sunday that negotiations over how to rescue Bear had continued throughout the weekend. He defended the Fed’s Friday bailout as “the right decision” and said the Bush administration was prepared to take additional action to stabilize financial markets.

Paulson declined to say what might have happened had the government failed to intervene.

“I’m not going to speculate about what-ifs,” he said. “I’m just going to say our clear priority right now—our number one priority, everything we’re doing in the economic arena—is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy.”

Bear Stearns has approximately 14,000 employees worldwide.

The deal marks an inglorious chapter in the history of 85-year-old Bear Stearns, a storied Wall Street firm whose unraveling has been both swift and dramatic.

Rumors that Bear Stearns was on the verge of collapse began circulating across Wall Street trading desks the previous Monday. Chief Executive Alan Schwartz—who succeeded longtime chief Jimmy Cayne in early January—appeared on television Wednesday afternoon to reassure the markets that the firm was stable.

By Thursday night, however, Bear was facing a severe liquidity crunch. Some firms that traded with Bear effectively stopped extending credit because they feared the company was running short of short-term funding, or liquidity.

“The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns,” said Schwartz, Bear Stearns’ president and CEO. “This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances.”

White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson had briefed U.S. President George W. Bush on the Federal Reserve’s role in facilitating the acquisition.

“We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening,” Fratto said. “Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments.”

Bear Stearns shares opened the previous week at $69.75. The stock had traded as high as $159 during the prior year.

The transaction was estimated at $236 million, placing Bear Stearns’ value at only $2 per share. Its stock had ended Friday at $30 after losing 47% during that session.

JPMorgan said it would immediately guarantee the trading commitments of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries while also assuming oversight of the company’s operations. Although the Federal Reserve and other regulators had already approved the agreement, Bear Stearns shareholders still needed to endorse it. The expedited acquisition was expected to be completed by the end of June.

As part of the arrangement, the Fed agreed to provide emergency funding covering as much as $30 billion of Bear Stearns’ assets.

JPMorgan Chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon emphasized that his company was backing Bear Stearns and said the investment bank’s customers and counterparties could be confident that JPMorgan was guaranteeing the associated risk.

Bear Stearns had come close to financial failure on Friday. JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York responded by arranging a short-term loan for the brokerage. The firm was experiencing the equivalent of a traditional bank run: short-term lenders stopped extending new credit while also demanding payment on existing obligations. Those simultaneous pressures exhausted Bear’s available cash.

With the worldwide credit crisis becoming more severe, the Federal Reserve, together with the Treasury Department and other government bodies, intervened to keep the investment bank from collapsing and potentially triggering panic across global financial markets.

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson said Sunday that negotiations over a Bear Stearns rescue had continued through the weekend. He described the Fed’s Friday intervention as the correct course of action and said the Bush administration was prepared to take further steps to stabilize financial markets. Paulson declined to predict what would have occurred without government involvement. Instead, he said the administration’s top economic objective was to limit instability and prevent financial-market turmoil from spreading into the broader economy.

Bear Stearns employed about 14,000 people around the world. Its sale represented a humiliating turn for the prominent 85-year-old Wall Street company, whose deterioration had occurred with remarkable speed.

Speculation that Bear Stearns was close to failing began circulating among Wall Street traders the previous Monday. On Wednesday afternoon, CEO Alan Schwartz appeared on television in an effort to convince investors that the firm remained sound. Schwartz had become chief executive in early January, replacing longtime leader Jimmy Cayne.

By Thursday night, however, Bear Stearns was facing an acute crisis. Some companies that conducted business with the firm essentially cut off credit because they believed it was running out of liquidity, or short-term financing.

Schwartz, who was Bear Stearns’ president and CEO, described the preceding week as extraordinarily difficult. Given the circumstances, he said, the JPMorgan agreement offered the best available result for everyone with an interest in the company.

White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson had updated President George W. Bush about the Federal Reserve’s part in facilitating the acquisition. Fratto said the White House welcomed the Fed’s actions and noted that Paulson and Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke were closely involved in responding to problems in the financial markets. He added that Paulson had kept the president informed about the latest developments.

Bear Stearns shares had begun the previous week at $69.75. During the prior year, the stock had traded as high as $159.

counterfactuals.output:
# JPMorgan to Buy Stricken Bear Stearns for $236 Million in Fed-Backed Rescue

**NEW YORK, March 16, 2008 —** JPMorgan Chase & Co. agreed Sunday to acquire Bear Stearns Cos. for about $236 million, a stunning collapse for one of Wall Street’s most prominent investment banks and an extraordinary government-backed effort to prevent a widening panic in global financial markets.

The all-stock deal values Bear Stearns at just **$2 a share**, based on JPMorgan’s closing share price Friday. Bear’s stock had finished the week at $30 and traded above $170 early last year, before losses tied to subprime mortgages and a deepening credit crisis eroded confidence in the firm.

The transaction was negotiated under intense pressure over the weekend after Bear Stearns suffered what amounted to a run on the bank. Customers, trading partners and lenders pulled money or refused to extend financing, rapidly draining the short-term liquidity on which the investment bank depended.

To make the takeover possible, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York agreed to provide special financing for as much as **$30 billion of Bear Stearns assets**. The arrangement limits JPMorgan’s exposure to some of the mortgage-related and other less-liquid securities on Bear’s balance sheet.

The sale price is one of the clearest signs yet of the severity of the financial crisis. Bear Stearns, founded in 1923 and long known for its aggressive bond-trading culture, had a book value many times greater than JPMorgan’s offer and occupied a major position in the markets for mortgages, derivatives and securities financing.

## A run that unfolded in days

Bear Stearns’ immediate crisis accelerated during the past week as rumors about its financial condition spread across Wall Street.

Although Bear had reported billions of dollars in available liquidity, confidence evaporated quickly. Hedge-fund customers moved cash and trading accounts elsewhere. Counterparties demanded more collateral or became reluctant to trade with the firm. Short-term lenders pulled back, leaving Bear unable to fund itself normally.

On Friday, the Federal Reserve took the exceptional step of arranging emergency financing through JPMorgan. The New York Fed supplied the money, while JPMorgan acted as the intermediary because Bear Stearns, as an investment bank rather than a commercial bank, did not have ordinary access to the Fed’s discount window.

Bear said Friday that its liquidity position had “significantly deteriorated” during the previous 24 hours. The emergency loan bought negotiators time, but officials concluded that Bear could not open for business Monday without a permanent solution.

The weekend talks brought together senior executives from Bear Stearns and JPMorgan, along with officials from the Federal Reserve, the New York Fed and the Treasury Department. Regulators feared that a disorderly bankruptcy could send losses through the financial system because Bear was linked to banks, hedge funds and other institutions through vast numbers of derivatives and financing contracts.

## Dimon says JPMorgan will stand behind Bear

JPMorgan Chairman and Chief Executive Jamie Dimon said the acquisition was intended to reassure Bear Stearns’ customers and trading partners.

“**JPMorgan Chase stands behind Bear Stearns,**” Dimon said in announcing the agreement. He added that Bear’s clients and counterparties should feel secure because JPMorgan was guaranteeing the firm’s counterparty obligations.

JPMorgan said it would immediately guarantee Bear Stearns’ trading obligations and provide management oversight, even before shareholders vote on the transaction. The companies said they expected to complete the merger during the second quarter, subject to shareholder approval.

The acquisition would give JPMorgan Bear’s prime-brokerage business, trading operations and Manhattan headquarters. But the speed of the collapse—and the complexity of Bear’s balance sheet—made direct government support essential to the agreement.

The Federal Reserve financing is designed to protect JPMorgan from potentially severe losses on a pool of Bear assets whose value has become difficult to determine in frozen credit markets. The intervention puts public money behind a private takeover and is likely to ignite debate over whether the government is rescuing Wall Street firms from the consequences of excessive risk-taking.

## Schwartz calls sale the best available outcome

Bear Stearns Chief Executive Alan Schwartz described the sale as a painful but necessary response to circumstances that had overwhelmed the firm.

“**This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances,**” Schwartz said.

Schwartz had tried in recent days to reassure investors that Bear remained adequately capitalized. But the crisis was driven less by formal measures of capital than by the loss of confidence in the firm’s ability to obtain daily financing. Once counterparties began withdrawing, Bear’s cash reserves disappeared with extraordinary speed.

The $2-a-share price leaves shareholders with only a fraction of the value they held even at the end of last week. Employees are expected to be among the biggest losers because they own a substantial portion of Bear Stearns stock, often through compensation and retirement plans.

## Paulson and White House endorse emergency action

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson supported the rescue, portraying it as necessary to preserve stability and orderly market functioning.

Paulson said he was pleased with the actions taken by the Federal Reserve and the New York Fed, adding that the measures would strengthen the financial system and support orderly markets. Treasury officials emphasized that the decision was aimed at containing broader risks rather than protecting Bear Stearns’ shareholders, who are receiving a deeply discounted price.

The White House also welcomed the agreement and said President George W. Bush had been kept informed. Administration officials expressed support for Paulson and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke as they worked to limit the danger to the wider economy.

The administration’s response reflected concern that Bear’s failure could undermine already fragile confidence in banks and securities firms. Credit markets have been under stress since last summer, when losses on subprime mortgages began spreading through mortgage-backed securities, structured investment vehicles and bank balance sheets.

## Fed broadens its safety net

Alongside the Bear Stearns rescue, the Federal Reserve announced a new lending facility intended to provide short-term funding to major securities dealers. The move effectively extends a form of central-bank support beyond traditional commercial banks to investment firms that are central to the functioning of financial markets.

The facility will allow primary dealers to borrow against a broad range of collateral, beginning Monday. It marks a major expansion of the Fed’s role as lender of last resort and signals that policymakers believe the threat extends well beyond one institution.

Officials hope the combined measures—the JPMorgan takeover, the Fed-backed asset financing and the new dealer-lending program—will calm markets before trading opens in Asia and Europe.

Still, the rescue is likely to intensify questions about the financial condition of other Wall Street firms, the value of mortgage-related assets and the adequacy of regulation for investment banks that rely heavily on short-term borrowing.

For Bear Stearns, the agreement represents a near-total destruction of shareholder value in less than a week. For the Federal Reserve and the Treasury, it is an unprecedented attempt to stop the failure of a major securities firm from becoming a systemic financial crisis.
